summary: Describes a DDDS database that uses the DNS to store rules, with domain names as keys and the rules encoded as NAPTR records. It replaces RFC 2915 and so is the official specification for the NAPTR resource record.

plainLanguage.summary: DDDS needs somewhere to keep its rules, so it uses the internet's phone book, DNS. NAPTR is the kind of entry that holds each rule.

subtitle: How the DNS stores delegation rules as NAPTR records, so a string can be rewritten step by step into a domain name.

tldr.problem: The Dynamic Delegation Discovery System (DDDS) needs a place to keep its rewrite rules, and the rules must be changeable and re-delegable over time.
tldr.mechanism: The DNS acts as the rule database: a domain name is the key, and the rules come back as NAPTR resource records that hold a regular expression or a replacement domain name.
tldr.outcome: RFC 3403 obsoletes RFC 2915 and RFC 2168, so it is the official specification of the NAPTR record. It defines no application of its own; applications such as ENUM and URI resolution supply the flags and services.

today: RFC 3403 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 2915 and RFC 2168, and no later RFC is recorded as obsoleting or updating it. It is therefore the specification of the NAPTR record that this site lists, and it is read together with RFC 3401 and RFC 3402.

sections.title: Why DDDS Uses the DNS
sections.content:
The Dynamic Delegation Discovery System (DDDS) does lazy binding of strings to data. It maps a unique string to data in a database by applying string transformation rules again and again until a terminal condition is reached. This RFC is Part Three of a series that RFC 3401 specifies as a whole, and the RFC stresses that no document in the series can be understood without reading the others.

RFC 3403 describes how the Domain Name System stores the rules. It does not specify any application. The NAPTR (Naming Authority Pointer) record it defines began in the URN Working Group as a way to encode rule sets in the DNS, so that delegated sections of a URI could be changed and re-delegated over time. Each record carries a regular expression, chosen for its compactness to expressivity ratio, so a lot of information fits in a small DNS packet.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine a treasure hunt where each clue tells you where the next clue is. DNS is the place where all the clues are filed, and this RFC says how to write them down.

sections.title: The DDDS Database in the DNS
sections.content:
The RFC fills in the standard parts of a DDDS database. A key is a validly constructed DNS domain name. A lookup is an ordinary DNS request for NAPTR records at that name, and the response is a series of NAPTR records. Rules are inserted by adding records to the right DNS zone, and only whoever controls a zone can set the rule for a key in it.

Values in NAPTR records use UTF-8. Non-ASCII input or output must be read as code points rather than bytes, and substitution expressions MUST NOT depend on a specific POSIX locale. Because every DNS record has a time to live (TTL), a rule can expire. If a client falls back to rules it fetched earlier, it MUST make sure none of them has expired, and if even one has, it must start the algorithm over.

Two applications may share the database, as ENUM and URI resolution do. To avoid collisions the RFC offers three ways: put each application's records in its own zone (for example urires.example.com and enum.example.com), anchor the regular expression so it matches only one application's strings, or use different Flags or Services values so another application's records are ignored.
sections.plainLanguage: The key is a name, and asking DNS about that name hands back a stack of rule cards. Only the owner of the name can add cards, and old cards must be thrown away when they expire.

sections.title: The NAPTR Record
sections.content:
The DNS type code for NAPTR is 35. A record has six fields:

  • ORDER: a 16-bit unsigned integer giving the order in which records MUST be processed, lowest to highest. Records with the same order count as the same rule.
  • PREFERENCE: a 16-bit unsigned integer that orders records with equal Order, low before high, like the preference in an MX record. It is the Priority of the DDDS Algorithm.
  • FLAGS: a character string of single characters from A-Z and 0-9, case not significant, possibly empty. The application defines them and says which are terminal.
  • SERVICES: a character string of Service Parameters, defined by the application.
  • REGEXP: a substitution expression applied to the original string to build the next domain name to look up.
  • REPLACEMENT: the next domain name to query, used when the rewrite is a simple replacement. It MUST be fully qualified and name compression is not used.

REGEXP and REPLACEMENT together make up the substitution expression and are mutually exclusive. A record with values in both is in error and SHOULD be ignored or an error returned. Regular expressions MUST NOT be used cumulatively: they apply to the original string, never to the name produced by an earlier rewrite, which the RFC says has proved extremely fault sensitive and hard to debug.

In a master file, Order and Preference are integers from 0 to 65535, and Flags, Services and Regexp are quoted character strings.
sections.plainLanguage: Each rule card says what number it is in the line, what kind of thing it is about, and how to turn what you have into the next address to visit.

sections.title: Processing Records and Applications
sections.content:
A client MUST process NAPTR records in the order given by the Order field. It MUST NOT simply use the first record that offers a Service Parameter combination it knows. Once a match is found, the client MUST NOT consider records with a different Order, though it MAY consider those with the same Order and different Preferences. If a lookup after a rewrite fails, clients are strongly encouraged to report a failure rather than back up to try other rewrite paths.

For load balancing among otherwise equal services, the RFC points to other DNS mechanisms such as SRV records or multiple A records, not Preference.

On the server side, DNS servers MAY add relevant records, generally A and SRV, to the additional section. Applications MAY look there but MUST NOT require it, since many servers never fill it in. An application that uses this database must also say which domain its first key belongs to, which Services and Protocols values are allowed, and what the terminal rule produces and how Flags are used.
sections.plainLanguage: You must read the rule cards in number order and stop at the first one that fits. If the next step leads nowhere, say so instead of wandering back to try other paths.

sections.title: Worked Examples: URN and ENUM
sections.content:
The URN example is marked as hypothetical. For the URN urn:cid:199606121851.1@bar.example.com, the first rule takes the text between the first and second colon, cid, and appends urn.arpa to get the key cid.urn.arpa. The single NAPTR record there has an empty flags field, so its regular expression is applied to the whole URN, yields example.com, and the lookup is not terminal. Records at example.com carry the flag a, which this application defines as terminal: the output is a domain name to query for an A record.

In the ENUM example the telephone number +1-770-555-1212 becomes the key 17705551212. ENUM inserts periods between digits, reverses the key and appends e164.arpa, giving 2.1.2.1.5.5.5.0.7.7.1.e164.arpa.. The records returned use the u flag, meaning the rule is terminal and the output is a URI, and offer SIP and SMTP mail as ways to reach the service.
sections.plainLanguage: For a phone number, you flip the digits, add dots, and ask DNS. The answer is a card that says how to reach that person, for example by a SIP call or an email.

sections.title: Advice for DNS Administrators
sections.content:
Regular expressions are hard to get right, and they interact badly with zone file syntax. Because backslash is the escape character, any backslash in a regexp must be entered twice in a zone file to appear once in the query response. The RFC warns that the need for double backslashes has probably not been tested by all DNS server implementors.

To reduce the number of backslashes, administrators should encourage rule writers to use the default delimiter feature: the regular expression starts with the character that serves as delimiter, so beginning with an exclamation mark usually needs fewer backslashes.
sections.plainLanguage: Backslashes are tricky: you have to write each one twice so it comes out once. Starting the rule with an exclamation mark helps you write fewer of them.

sections.title: Security and IANA Notes
sections.content:
A NAPTR record, like any DNS record, can be signed and validated with DNSSEC. The RFC adds that the database makes identifiers from other namespaces subject to the same attacks as normal domain names. Since those identifiers were not easily resolvable before, this may or may not be a problem.

Regular expressions should be checked for sanity and not blindly passed to something like PERL, since arbitrary code can be included and then run. For IANA, the values of Services and Flags are decided by each application and may need a registration mechanism, but this specification by itself needs none.
sections.plainLanguage: Rule cards can be signed so you know they are real, and you should read a rule carefully before running it, because a sneaky rule could hide a harmful instruction.
